summary: Defines an XML document format for describing the media properties of SIP sessions, such as codecs and media types. It also defines an XML format for policies that limit those properties. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: This is a form for listing what kinds of sound and video a call uses, and another form for saying which kinds are allowed.

subtitle: An XML format for describing what media a SIP call uses, and for setting limits on codecs, media types, bandwidth and ports.

tldr.problem: Networks want to tell SIP user agents which codecs, media types, bandwidth and ports they may use, and user agents need a way to describe a session to a policy server.
tldr.mechanism: The Media Policy Data Set Format is one XML vocabulary with two root elements: session-info describes a specific session, and session-policy states rules that apply to sessions in general.
tldr.outcome: Policy documents from several sources can be merged by combining their restrictions, so a session must satisfy all of them. If the sets of allowed codecs do not overlap, no session can be set up.

facts.label: Bandwidth unit
facts.value: kilobits per second (1024 bits per second)

today: RFC 6796 is a Proposed Standard and the data shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is used together with the session policy framework in RFC 6794 and the user agent profile framework in RFC 6080.

sections.title: Why a Media Policy Format
sections.content:
Two frameworks, RFC 6080 (user agent profile delivery) and RFC 6794 (SIP session policies), define how a network server conveys configuration and policy to a SIP user agent (UA). An important part of that information is about media: which codecs and media types a session may use, which media intermediaries it must pass through, and how much bandwidth is available.

RFC 6796 defines the Media Policy Data Set Format (MPDF) for this information. It is used in two ways. A session info document describes the properties of a given session and is usually built from its session description. A session policy document sets rules for sessions independent of any specific session description.

Both document types share the same set of XML elements. They differ in their root element: <session-info> for session information and <session-policy> for policies.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of paper. One describes the call you are making right now. The other is a list of house rules for any call.

sections.title: Format Basics and Common Attributes
sections.content:
An MPDF document is XML 1.0, MUST be well-formed and valid against the available schemas, and MUST be encoded in UTF-8. The namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:mediadataset and the media type is application/media-policy-dataset+xml. Elements or attributes from unknown namespaces MUST be ignored, which is how the format is extended.

Several attributes can appear on many elements:

  • visibility: visible (the default) or hidden, advising the UA not to show the value to the user.
  • direction: sendrecv (the default), sendonly or recvonly, limiting a property to one direction.
  • q: a preference from 0 to 1 with at most two decimal places; higher is preferred. It is only allowed on elements that list allowed values.
  • media-type: limits an element to streams of one type such as audio or video.
  • label: a token that identifies a stream and MUST be unique among the <stream> elements of a session info document.
  • enabled: yes (the default) or no; with no the UA MUST NOT establish the stream.

If an element carries an attribute that is not permitted for it, the UA MUST ignore the attribute.
sections.eli5: Each rule can carry little stickers: hide this from the user, this only applies when sending, or this choice is my favorite.

sections.title: Session Info Documents
sections.content:
A session info document describes one SIP session. A UA builds it from its SDP session description or from an SDP offer/answer pair, sends it to a policy server, and the server returns a version that complies with its policies. For example, if video is not permitted and the document contains a video stream, the server sets enabled="no" on that stream. A server can reject a session completely by returning an empty <session-info> element.

The mapping from SDP is strict. The UA MUST create one <stream> element for each m= line, in the same order, with a <media-type> and a <codec> for each codec listed. The q values on the codecs MUST decrease in the order the codecs appear in the m= line. The address and port from the c= and m= lines go into <local-host-port>, and the remote side, if known, goes into <remote-host-port>. A b=CT line sets <max-bw>, and a b=AS line sets <max-session-bw> or <max-stream-bw> depending on whether it is at session or media level. An a=label attribute sets the stream label.

The remote address can be sensitive, so a UA configured not to disclose it leaves out <remote-host-port>.
sections.eli5: The UA writes down each sound or picture channel of the call, in order, and the server can cross one out if it is not allowed.

sections.title: Media Intermediaries
sections.content:
The <media-intermediaries> element tells the UA to send media through a chain of intermediaries, in the order listed, topmost first. Because different intermediary types are not necessarily interoperable, an element SHOULD contain intermediaries of one type only. The RFC notes this is a policy for which intermediaries to traverse and is not meant to replace connectivity discovery such as ICE.

Three types are defined:

  • <fixed-intermediary>: relies on pre-configured forwarding rules. The UA sends media to the first intermediary, given by <int-host-port> and optional <int-addl-port> elements.
  • <turn-intermediary>: a TURN relay, with optional <shared-secret>, <user> and <transport> elements. If no transport is given, UDP is assumed; tcp and udp are defined.
  • <msrp-intermediary>: an MSRP relay named by an <msrp-uri>, whose scheme MUST be msrps:.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the rules say your call must go through certain stops on the way, like a package passing through specific depots.

sections.title: Session Policy Elements
sections.content:
A session policy document is created by a policy server and passed to a UA, which applies it to the sessions it sets up. For example, if video is prohibited, the UA leaves video out of its SDP offer or answer.

The main elements are:

  • <media-types-allowed> and <media-types-excluded>: a whitelist or blacklist of media types. The two MUST NOT appear in the same container.
  • <codecs-allowed> and <codecs-excluded>: the same for codecs. A policy MUST allow at least one codec per media type.
  • <local-ports>: a range such as 1-65535 (the default), inclusive, with port numbers from 1 to 65535. A start port greater than the end port allows no sessions.
  • <max-bw>, <max-session-bw> and <max-stream-bw>: bandwidth limits in kilobits per second (1024 bits per second) that include lower-layer overhead such as UDP and IP.
  • <qos-dscp>: a DSCP value from 0 to 63 for the IP DS field of media packets.
  • <context>: who issued the document, with optional policy server URI, contact, human-readable info and an opaque token used to build a Policy-ID header.

A codec is written as a <media-type-subtype> such as audio/PCMA, optionally with <mime-parameter> name=value pairs (for example profile=0) to single out one encoding or profile.
sections.eli5: The rules can say which kinds of sound and picture are okay, how much internet the call may use, and which doors, called ports, it may open.

sections.title: Merging Policies from Several Sources
sections.content:
A UA may receive session policy documents from multiple sources. They can be merged into one document that expresses the logical AND of the policies. The merging rules are part of each element's semantics, so a generic tool cannot merge documents without understanding every element in them.

  • Sets of media types and codecs: the UA applies each container in any order to the set it supports, and the set must stay the same or shrink. Nothing can be added.
  • Single values: the lowest <max-bw>, <max-session-bw> or <max-stream-bw> MUST be used.
  • Ports: the permitted ranges are intersected.
  • DSCP and context: the DSCP value comes from the local policy server, and the merged <context> is determined by local policy.

The RFC's example: a UA supports PCMA, PCMU and G729. One policy excludes PCMA, leaving PCMU and G729. A second policy allows only PCMA and G729, so the result is G729. If two policies allow non-overlapping sets, the merged set would be empty, which the schema forbids. That is a conflict that cannot be resolved automatically, and the UA will not be able to set up a session.
sections.eli5: If two grown-ups give you different rules, you follow both. If their rules cannot both be followed, you cannot play at all.

sections.title: Security and Registrations
sections.content:
Session info and policy information can be sensitive, so the protocol that distributes them SHOULD provide authentication, confidentiality and message integrity. The RFC says that using RFC 6795 meets these requirements. A UA should only accept policies from servers it is configured to trust and should check the server's certificate.

An attacker could modify policy documents, or send fake ones, to make processing more costly for the client or to get the client to follow fake policies as part of a denial-of-service attack. The <shared-secret> element carries a secret for authenticating to a media intermediary, so documents containing it MUST be kept private in transit, and when RFC 6795 is used, TLS or S/MIME encryption MUST be used.

For IANA, the RFC registers the media type application/media-policy-dataset+xml, a RELAX NG schema (the schema is given in Section 8 of the RFC), and the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:mediadataset.
sections.eli5: These papers can hold secrets, so they should travel in a locked box, and you should only trust rules from people you expect to hear from.
